0.title: The Person You Find Hard
0.essay:
A name came to mind when you read the title. Perhaps it is the colleague who corrects everything you do, the relative whose visits you dread for a week beforehand, the church member who leaves you drained, or the neighbour who flares up over nothing.

Everyone has someone

The Bible does not pretend that people are easy. Its pages are full of hard characters: Laban the cheat, Nabal the brute, Saul with his spear, Diotrephes who had to be first. God’s people have always had to live, work and worship beside them.

And each of us is someone’s

It does begin, though, where Jesus begins. “Why do you see the speck that is in your brother’s eye, but do not notice the log that is in your own eye?” (Matthew 7:3). Somewhere, someone finds me hard to be with. That is humbling, and it is also the start of hope, because the God who is patient with difficult people has been patient with me.

Neither doormat nor fighter

With a hard person we tend to do one of two things. We give way every time and call it love, or we fight back and call it honesty. The gospel opens a third path: a love strong enough to do good to someone who is hard, and free enough to say no to them.

The study Getting On with People sets out the general principles for every relationship, and the study Handling Conflict covers the hard conversation itself. This study builds on both: it is about the person who stays hard.

One thing must be said at the start. A difficult person is not the same as an abusive or dangerous one. If someone is harming or frightening you, turn first to the chapter Love with Limits.

The chapters

First, My Own Heart; Six Hard Kinds of People; How Jesus Dealt with Difficult People; Love with Limits; The Ones You Cannot Leave; and In the Moment and Afterwards.

For reflection

Who came to mind as you began? And who might name you, if they were asked the same question?

1.title: First, My Own Heart
1.essay:
When someone is hard to be with, all our attention goes to them: what they said, what they meant, what they will do next. The Bible gently turns us round. Before I can deal wisely with this person, I need to know what this person does to me.

What they stir up

Think of your difficult person, and notice what rises in you. For some of us it is fear: a tight chest when their name appears on the phone. For others it is anger, hot or cold. Often it is the wish to be right, to have them admit for once that we had a point. Or it is the wish to be liked, so strong that we agree to things we resent an hour later.

None of these was put into us by the other person. A difficult person is like a hand squeezing a sponge: what comes out was already inside. The studies The Fear of Man and Anger look closely at two of these reactions.

This is not taking the blame

Looking at my own heart does not mean their behaviour is my fault. Their sin is theirs. If they are rude, the rudeness belongs to them, and God holds them to account for it. But my response belongs to me. I cannot repent for them. I can only bring one heart to God, and it is the only one he asks me to bring. “Search me, O God, and know my heart! Try me and know my thoughts!” (Psalm 139:23).

God’s unlikely tool

Here is a thought we would not have chosen. God uses difficult people to make us like his Son. “We rejoice in our sufferings, knowing that suffering produces endurance, and endurance produces character, and character produces hope” (Romans 5:3–4). James says the same: “the testing of your faith produces steadfastness. And let steadfastness have its full effect, that you may be perfect and complete, lacking in nothing” (James 1:3–4).

Patience cannot grow where there is nothing to be patient with. Gentleness is only learned near someone who is harsh. We pray to become more loving, and God, who takes that prayer seriously, sends us somebody hard to love. This does not make their behaviour good. It means that their behaviour cannot spoil what God is doing. He has promised that for those who love him “all things work together for good”, and the good he has in mind is that we should be “conformed to the image of his Son” (Romans 8:28–29).

An image-bearer with a story

When someone hurts us often enough, they shrink in our minds into a single word: the bully, the moaner, the control freak. Scripture will not let us leave them there. James is appalled that with the tongue “we curse people who are made in the likeness of God” (James 3:9). The person you find hard was made by God, bears his image, and has a story you probably know only in part. The sharp critic may have grown up never once being praised. The one who must control everything may be very frightened underneath.

A story explains. It does not excuse. But it changes the way we look at someone, and it is hard to deal wisely with a person we have stopped seeing as a person.

Pray for them

Jesus gives one command about hard people that we can obey today, whatever they do. “Love your enemies and pray for those who persecute you, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun rise on the evil and on the good” (Matthew 5:44–45). Luke records it this way: “bless those who curse you, pray for those who abuse you” (Luke 6:28).

Do not pray only that they would change, though you may ask that. Pray for their good: their health, their family, their soul. It is very difficult to go on hating someone you pray for by name each morning.

Loved while we were difficult

Where does the strength for this come from? Not from trying harder to be nice. It comes from remembering how God has treated us. “God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8). Paul goes further: “while we were enemies we were reconciled to God by the death of his Son” (Romans 5:10). We were not merely awkward towards God. We were against him. And he did not keep his distance until we improved. He came near, at the cost of his Son’s blood.

Think how patient God has been with you this week alone: the prayers you forgot, the sins you repeated, the grumbling he heard. He has not once rolled his eyes. This is the love we now stand in, and it is the only well deep enough to draw from when someone is hard to love.

An example

A man dreads his team meeting each Monday because one colleague interrupts him and picks holes in everything he says. For months he has replayed these meetings on the drive home, composing clever replies. One evening he asks himself a different question: why does this get to me so much? He realises that he badly wants to be thought competent, and this colleague threatens it. He begins to pray for the colleague by name before each meeting. The interruptions do not stop, but the drive home becomes quieter, and he finds he can answer a fair point without his voice shaking.

For reflection

What does your difficult person stir up in you: fear, anger, the need to be right, or the need to be liked? What might that show you about what you are relying on? What do you know of their story? Will you pray for their good, by name, each day this week?

2.title: Six Hard Kinds of People
2.essay:
Difficult people are not all difficult in the same way, and what helps with one can make things worse with another. Scripture gives us portraits of several kinds, with wisdom for each. A warning first: these are portraits to help us understand, not labels to dismiss anyone with. Most of us are at least one of them on a bad day.

The critic

Some people find fault with everything. When David fled Jerusalem, a man named Shimei walked beside the road cursing him and throwing stones. David’s soldiers wanted to silence him. David said, “Leave him alone, and let him curse” (2 Samuel 16:11). He did not need to win, because he had put his case in God’s hands: “It may be that the LORD will look on the wrong done to me” (2 Samuel 16:12).

With a critic, listen for the grain of truth, take it, and leave the rest. “Do not take to heart all the things that people say, lest you hear your servant cursing you. Your heart knows that many times you yourself have cursed others” (Ecclesiastes 7:21–22). Not every criticism needs an answer.

The controller

Others must be in charge. In one early church there was “Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first” (3 John 9). He refused to welcome travelling Christians and “stops those who want to and puts them out of the church” (3 John 10). The apostle John did not shrug. “I will bring up what he is doing” (3 John 10). Control in a church is to be named, and brought to those responsible.

Jacob worked for another controller, his uncle Laban, who “cheated me and changed my wages ten times” (Genesis 31:7). Jacob served faithfully for twenty years, and then, at God’s word, he left. With a controlling person, be clear in your own mind about what is theirs to decide and what is not, and say a calm no to the second.

The angry

Some people explode. “A soft answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger” (Proverbs 15:1). Proverbs adds a caution about closeness: “Make no friendship with a man given to anger, nor go with a wrathful man, lest you learn his ways and entangle yourself in a snare” (Proverbs 22:24–25). Anger is catching.

Nabal was such a man. His own servant said that “one cannot speak to him” (1 Samuel 25:17). His wife Abigail, whose story is told in the study Handling Conflict, shows one overlooked piece of wisdom: timing. She came home to find him drunk, and “she told him nothing at all until the morning light” (1 Samuel 25:36). Never try to reason with someone in the middle of a rage. Wait until the storm has passed.

The deceiver

Harder to spot is the person who is charming to your face and works against you behind your back. “Whoever hates disguises himself with his lips and harbors deceit in his heart; when he speaks graciously, believe him not” (Proverbs 26:24–25). This is not a licence to suspect everyone. It is permission to believe what you have seen. Watch what a person does more than what they say. Keep important things in writing, and have someone else present for the conversations that matter. Jesus sent his disciples out to be “wise as serpents and innocent as doves” (Matthew 10:16): not naive, and not cynical.

The taker

Then there is the person who always needs something, or always has a complaint. Moses led a nation of complainers, and it nearly broke him. “I am not able to carry all this people alone; the burden is too heavy for me” (Numbers 11:14). God did not tell him to try harder. He gave seventy elders to share the weight.

Paul helps us here with two sentences that sound like a contradiction. “Bear one another’s burdens” (Galatians 6:2). And three verses later: “each will have to bear his own load” (Galatians 6:5). A burden is a weight too heavy for one person: a bereavement, an illness, a crisis. A load is the ordinary pack each of us must carry. Love helps with burdens. It does not carry a load that someone could and should carry themselves, and it does not try to be anyone’s saviour. There is only one of those.

The one who will not listen

Last, the person who cannot be told. Proverbs is blunt: “Do not reprove a scoffer, or he will hate you; reprove a wise man, and he will love you” (Proverbs 9:8). Then it sets two proverbs side by side. “Answer not a fool according to his folly, lest you be like him yourself” (Proverbs 26:4). “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he be wise in his own eyes” (Proverbs 26:5).

They sit together on purpose. Sometimes replying only drags you down to the same level, and silence is wise. Sometimes silence would let a falsehood stand and others would be harmed, and you must speak. No rule tells you which. That takes wisdom, and God “gives generously to all without reproach” (James 1:5) when we ask for it.

An example

A woman’s elderly neighbour telephones every evening, sometimes for an hour, with a long list of complaints about the council, his family and his health. She has begun to dread the ring. Thinking it over, she sees that he has real burdens: he cannot drive, and he is lonely. She also sees that she has been carrying his whole load of grievances, which she cannot fix. She tells him kindly that she will ring him on Tuesdays and Saturdays, and she offers to drive him to his hospital appointments. He grumbles at first. But she finds she can now listen to him gladly, and he has started asking how she is.

For reflection

Which of these portraits is closest to the person you find hard? Which is closest to you, on a bad day? Is there a criticism you have received that contains a grain of truth? Are you carrying a load that belongs to someone else?

3.title: How Jesus Dealt with Difficult People
3.essay:
Nobody has had to deal with more difficult people than Jesus. Enemies tried to trap him, crowds pressed on him, friends corrected him, his family thought him mad, and one of his own sold him. Watching how he responded is the best education there is. It is also more than an education, as we shall see.

The trap: calm truth and a question

The Pharisees “plotted how to entangle him in his words” (Matthew 22:15). Is it lawful to pay taxes to Caesar, or not? Either answer would ruin him. Jesus saw it clearly: “aware of their malice” (Matthew 22:18), he did not pretend the question was innocent. But he did not lose his temper or walk off either. He asked for a coin, and then asked a question of his own: “Whose likeness and inscription is this?” (Matthew 22:20). His answer left them with nothing to say.

The crowd: withdrawing to pray

The crowds were not hostile, only endless. Everyone wanted something. After one exhausting evening of healing, “rising very early in the morning, while it was still dark, he departed and went out to a desolate place, and there he prayed” (Mark 1:35). When the disciples found him with the news that everyone was looking for him, he did not go back. He went on to the next towns, because that was what his Father had sent him to do.

The Son of God, in his real humanity, did not meet every demand made on him. Stepping away to pray is not selfish. It was how Jesus kept doing his Father’s will, and not merely what the loudest voice wanted.

The friend who was wrong

When Jesus spoke of his coming death, Peter “took him aside and began to rebuke him” (Matthew 16:22). Peter meant well. He was also completely wrong, and Jesus said so at once: “You are a hindrance to me. For you are not setting your mind on the things of God, but on the things of man” (Matthew 16:23). There was no sulking and no hinting. The plain word was spoken, and the friendship went on. Six days later Peter was on the mountain with him.

The family who misunderstood

His own relatives once set out to take charge of him, “for they were saying, ‘He is out of his mind’” (Mark 3:21). John adds that “not even his brothers believed in him” (John 7:5). Jesus did not let his family steer his calling. He also never stopped loving them. From the cross he made sure his mother would be cared for (John 19:26–27). And after the resurrection we find his brothers among the believers at prayer (Acts 1:14). The relative who misunderstands you now may not always do so.

The betrayer at the table

Jesus knew what Judas was. He did not hide what he knew: he said openly at supper that one of them would betray him. And yet that same evening he “began to wash the disciples’ feet” (John 13:5), Judas’s among them. In the garden, with the kiss still on his cheek, he said, “Friend, do what you came to do” (Matthew 26:50). Jesus was never taken in by anyone. Early in his ministry he “did not entrust himself to them, because he knew all people” (John 2:24). But knowing the worst about a person never stopped him doing them good.

The mocker: silence

Herod had long wanted to see Jesus, “hoping to see some sign done by him” (Luke 23:8). He wanted a show, not the truth. “He questioned him at some length, but he made no answer” (Luke 23:9). Some people are not asking in order to learn. Jesus owed Herod no performance, and gave him none.

The cross

Then came the hardest people of all: those who drove in the nails and stood round to jeer. “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). Peter, who watched that night begin, later described it: “When he was reviled, he did not revile in return; when he suffered, he did not threaten, but continued entrusting himself to him who judges justly” (1 Peter 2:23).

That last phrase is the secret. Jesus could stay silent and unrevenged because he had handed his cause to his Father. Peter says that in this Christ was “leaving you an example, so that you might follow in his steps” (1 Peter 2:21).

More than an example

If Jesus were only our example, this chapter would crush us. Who answers like that? But Peter does not stop there. “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree” (1 Peter 2:24). We were not standing beside Jesus that day as fellow sufferers. We were among the difficult people. He bore our harsh words, our scheming and our cold shoulders, and he prayed for our forgiveness. Wonder at it: the one who has every right to find us impossible has made us his friends.

Notice too that Jesus had no single method. He answered, asked, withdrew, rebuked, served and kept silent, as each moment required. We need that same wisdom. And since, unlike him, we cannot read hearts, we should be slower than he was to decide what someone’s motives are.

An example

At every family gathering a woman’s brother-in-law makes sneering remarks about her faith. She has always either bitten back or gone quiet and fumed. This year she prays beforehand and decides to do neither. When the first remark comes, she smiles and asks, “Do you really want to know what I think, or are you teasing?” He is thrown, and mutters that he is teasing. She lets it go and passes the potatoes. Later, washing up, he asks her a real question.

For reflection

Which of these scenes speaks most to your situation? Do you tend to answer when silence would be wiser, or stay silent when a plain word is needed? What would it mean to entrust your cause to “him who judges justly”? How does it change things to remember that Christ bore your sins against him?

4.title: Love with Limits
4.essay:
Many Christians believe that loving a difficult person means putting up with anything. Others, worn out, decide that love has run its course and it is time to hit back. Romans 12 marks out a better path, and it is narrower and wiser than either.

What is ruled out: revenge

“Repay no one evil for evil” (Romans 12:17). “Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God” (Romans 12:19). Revenge is not only the dramatic kind. It is the cutting remark, the story told to make them look bad, the help quietly withheld, the long frost. All of it is forbidden.

The reason is not that their wrong does not matter. It matters so much that God himself will deal with it. Every sin will be justly answered, either at the cross, where Christ bore it for those who trust him, or at the last day. I am not the judge, and I am free to stop behaving like one.

What is commanded: good

Paul then says something startling. “If your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for by so doing you will heap burning coals on his head” (Romans 12:20). The coals are most likely the burning shame that unexpected kindness can bring, the kind that may lead to a change of heart. “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Romans 12:21). When I become bitter because of a hard person, evil has won twice.

Two honest words

In the middle of this stands a realistic sentence: “If possible, so far as it depends on you, live peaceably with all” (Romans 12:18). If possible: sometimes it is not. So far as it depends on you: part of it does not. God holds you responsible for your half of the relationship. He does not hold you responsible for theirs.

Limits are part of love

Love seeks the other person’s real good. It is not good for anyone to be allowed to shout, sneer or take without end. So a limit, rightly set, is an act of love and not a withdrawal of it.

How can you tell a limit from a punishment? A punishment says, “I will make you pay.” A limit says, “I will not take part in this.” A limit protects something good: your family, your health, the relationship itself. A limit is also about what you will do, since that is all you control. “If the shouting starts, I will leave the room, and we can talk when it is calm” is a limit. “You had better not shout at me again” is only a threat.

Jesus taught plain speech: “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). A Christian may say no without a long defence. When Jacob and Laban finally parted, they piled up stones as a marker, and Laban said, “I will not pass over this heap to you, and you will not pass over this heap and this pillar to me, to do harm” (Genesis 31:52). It was not warm friendship. It was an agreed line between two men who could not trust each other, and it kept the peace.

Truth, and other people’s help

Love tells the truth, “speaking the truth in love” (Ephesians 4:15). The study Handling Conflict explains how to go to someone privately and what to do if they will not hear. One point matters here. Jesus’ steps in Matthew 18 mean that you are not meant to bear a hard person alone. “If he does not listen, take one or two others along with you” (Matthew 18:16). And in the church a limit is sometimes commanded: “As for a person who stirs up division, after warning him once and then twice, have nothing more to do with him” (Titus 3:10).

When distance is wise

“The prudent sees danger and hides himself, but the simple go on and suffer for it” (Proverbs 22:3). Stepping back is sometimes simply prudent. Paul wrote, “Alexander the coppersmith did me great harm; the Lord will repay him according to his deeds. Beware of him yourself” (2 Timothy 4:14–15). Paul leaves revenge to the Lord and warns his friend to be careful, both at once. You can forgive someone from the heart and still not hand them your trust, your secrets or your house keys. The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation explains why forgiving and trusting are not the same thing.

Difficult, or dangerous?

Everything in this study is about people who are hard to be with. It is not about people who are harming you. If someone hits you, threatens you, forces or pressures you sexually, controls your money, your movements or whom you may see, or wears you down with constant contempt so that you live in fear, that is abuse. Abuse is not a difficulty to be borne with patience. No verse in this study asks you to stay within reach of it.

Your safety comes first. Get to a safe place. Tell someone you trust. Contact the police or a domestic abuse helpline, and in immediate danger call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America). If a child is being harmed or is at risk, report it to the authorities at once. Using the law is not unspiritual. Paul claimed his rights as a citizen to stop a flogging (Acts 22:25), and when he learned of a plot against his life he had it reported to the commander (Acts 23:16–17). The chapter on domestic violence and abuse in the study Biblical Counseling, and the study Divorce & Remarriage, say more.

An example

A woman’s sister sends her long, furious messages late at night whenever she feels slighted. For years the woman has stayed up answering each one, apologising for things she did not do. With a friend’s help she decides on a limit. She tells her sister, warmly and once: “I love you and I want to hear when you are upset. I will not answer messages like these. Ring me the next day and I will always pick up.” The next angry message comes within a week. She does not reply, and sleeps. Two days later her sister rings, stiff and offended, and they talk for the first time in months.

For reflection

Where have you been taking quiet revenge on someone? What small good could you do for a person who has been hard on you? Is there a limit you need to set, and can you state it in terms of what you will do? Is your situation difficult, or is it dangerous, and whom have you told?

5.title: The Ones You Cannot Leave
5.essay:
Advice about keeping your distance is little use when the difficult person sits at your breakfast table, signs your payslip, or shares your pew. Much of the Bible’s wisdom was written for exactly these people: the ones who are in our lives to stay.

A difficult parent

“Honor your father and your mother” (Exodus 20:12) has no age limit. Jesus rebuked those who found religious excuses to stop caring for their parents (Mark 7:10–13). But honouring is not the same as obeying. A grown son or daughter honours a parent by speaking respectfully, showing gratitude where it is due, and seeing that they are cared for. Honour does not mean letting a parent run your marriage, or agreeing to what is wrong. “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Jonathan shows what this looks like. His father Saul was jealous, unstable and bent on killing Jonathan’s closest friend. Jonathan would not join in. He spoke up plainly: “Why should he be put to death? What has he done?” (1 Samuel 20:32). He kept faith with David at great cost. And he did not abandon his father, but stayed at his side to the end. Loyal, but not obedient to sin.

A difficult marriage

Peter writes to wives whose husbands “do not obey the word”, that these men “may be won without a word by the conduct of their wives” (1 Peter 3:1). His point is that a steady, respectful life preaches more than constant argument. It does not mean a wife may never speak of what is wrong. It does not mean following a husband into sin. And it has nothing to do with enduring abuse, which the previous chapter addressed. The same passage commands husbands to “live with your wives in an understanding way, showing honor” (1 Peter 3:7), and Paul says, “Husbands, love your wives, and do not be harsh with them” (Colossians 3:19).

If your marriage is hard, do not wait for a crisis. Ask a pastor or a wise older couple for help early. The study Christian Marriage says much more.

A difficult boss or colleague

Peter told household servants to be respectful “not only to the good and gentle but also to the unjust” (1 Peter 2:18). “For this is a gracious thing, when, mindful of God, one endures sorrows while suffering unjustly” (1 Peter 2:19). Those servants had almost no legal protection, and Peter shows them how to live with dignity where they could not leave. The lasting lesson is that a hard boss does not release me from honest, respectful work, because I work “as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23).

It is not a command to accept every injustice in silence. An employee today may raise a concern, keep a record, use a grievance process or look for another job, and may do all of these without sin. The study Christian at Work has more on the workplace.

A difficult child, a difficult church member

Some of the deepest pain comes from a son or daughter, perhaps now grown, who is hostile or cold. The father in Jesus’ parable did not chase his son into the far country. He let him go, and he watched the road, so that “while he was still a long way off, his father saw him and felt compassion, and ran” (Luke 15:20).

In a church we are joined to people we did not choose. “Bearing with one another and, if one has a complaint against another, forgiving each other; as the Lord has forgiven you, so you also must forgive” (Colossians 3:13). Bearing with assumes that there will be something to bear. If a member’s behaviour is harming others, tell the elders. That is not gossip.

Joseph: wisdom through the long years

Joseph’s brothers sold him. More than twenty years later they stood before him, not knowing who he was, and he held all the power. He took no revenge. But he did not rush to embrace them either. He “treated them like strangers and spoke roughly to them” (Genesis 42:7), and tested them until he could see whether they had changed. Only then did he make himself known, and weep, and provide for them. Years on, he could say, “you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). Forgiveness was in his heart long before trust was rebuilt, and he saw God’s hand over the whole story.

David: no revenge, and out of range

David served a king who tried to pin him to the wall with a spear. Twice afterwards David had Saul at his mercy, and twice he refused to strike. “May the LORD judge between me and you, may the LORD avenge me against you, but my hand shall not be against you” (1 Samuel 24:12).

But notice the other half. When the spear flew, “David fled and escaped that night” (1 Samuel 19:10). He did not stand still out of duty. And when Saul later admitted his wrong and promised never to harm him again, David was courteous and did not move back to the palace. “David went his way, and Saul returned to his place” (1 Samuel 26:25). He honoured the king and he stayed out of reach of the spear. Scripture commends him for both.

David points beyond himself. His greater Son was also hated without cause, and also refused revenge. But where David escaped, Jesus did not. He stayed within range, and took the spear, for us.

An example

A woman in her fifties cares for her mother, who has always been sharp-tongued and has become more so with age. Every visit brings a list of her failings. She cannot walk away, and does not want to. She decides three things. She will go on visiting, cooking and managing the medical visits, as her honour to her mother before God. She will not argue with the insults or defend herself against them. And when the insults turn on her husband, she will say quietly, “I am not going to listen to that, Mum. I will come back on Thursday,” and go. Some weeks are still hard. But she no longer drives home in tears, and she has begun to thank God for her mother again.

For reflection

Who is the person you cannot leave? What would honour without obeying sin look like with them? Like David, how could you refuse revenge and also keep out of range? Where do you need someone’s help, and whom will you ask?

6.title: In the Moment and Afterwards
6.essay:
It is one thing to think clearly about a hard person on a quiet evening. It is another when they are in front of you, voice rising, and your heart is pounding. Here is some practical wisdom for that moment and for the hours that follow. None of it is a technique for winning. It is how people who are loved by God can behave when they are under pressure.

Pause and pray

Your body reacts before your mind does. So take one slow breath, and pray one sentence. David’s will do: “Set a guard, O LORD, over my mouth; keep watch over the door of my lips!” (Psalm 141:3).

Lower your voice

When they get louder, get quieter and slower. “With patience a ruler may be persuaded, and a soft tongue will break a bone” (Proverbs 25:15). A raised voice invites a raised voice, and “the anger of man does not produce the righteousness of God” (James 1:20).

Name the issue, not the person

Say what happened and what you are asking for. “The report went out without my section, and I would like to see drafts before they are sent” can be heard. “You always cut me out” cannot. Words like always and never are nearly always untrue, and they turn a problem into an attack. The study The Tongue has much more on this.

Ask a question

As Jesus so often did, ask. “What are you hoping I will do?” “Can you tell me what has upset you?” A sincere question slows things down and may uncover a real concern beneath the noise. “If one gives an answer before he hears, it is his folly and shame” (Proverbs 18:13).

Do not take the bait

Some remarks are thrown out to get a reaction. You do not have to give one. “The vexation of a fool is known at once, but the prudent ignores an insult” (Proverbs 12:16). You can let a jibe fall to the floor and return to the subject.

End it well

If the conversation is only getting hotter, stop it. “The beginning of strife is like letting out water, so quit before the quarrel breaks out” (Proverbs 17:14). Say something simple: “I want to sort this out, but not like this. Let us talk again tomorrow.” Then go, without a parting shot.

Afterwards: talk to God, then to one wise friend

You will want to replay it. Tell it to God first. “Pour out your heart before him; God is a refuge for us” (Psalm 62:8). Then, if you need to, talk to one wise and trustworthy friend. There is a clear difference between this and gossip. Gossip looks for allies and for an audience. A debrief looks for help: Was I fair? What should I do next? When David was hunted by Saul, Jonathan came and “strengthened his hand in God” (1 Samuel 23:16).

Forgive from the heart

“Whenever you stand praying, forgive, if you have anything against anyone” (Mark 11:25). Before God, release the debt, tonight, whether or not they ever apologise. With a difficult person you may have to do this again next week. The study Forgiveness & Reconciliation explains what forgiving does and does not mean.

The next day

Greet them as you normally would. If you spoke wrongly, apologise for your part plainly, without waiting for them to go first and without adding “but”. Do one small good thing for them. And if the matter still needs settling, arrange a time to settle it.

Guard against bitterness

The long-term danger with a difficult person is not what they do to your week. It is what resentment does to your soul. “See to it … that no ‘root of bitterness’ springs up and causes trouble, and by it many become defiled” (Hebrews 12:15). A root grows out of sight, and what it produces spreads to those around you.

The signs are familiar. You rehearse old conversations. You are quietly pleased when things go badly for them. You tell the story again to anyone who will listen. When you see these, do not simply resolve to stop. Do the opposite: pray for the person’s good, and thank God for one thing about them.

When it is wearing you down

Living or working beside a very hard person for a long time can affect your health: sleeplessness, constant dread, low mood. Seeing a doctor or a qualified counsellor is not a failure of faith, and medicine, where it is prescribed, is a good gift. If you ever have thoughts of harming yourself or ending your life, please get help now. Call the emergency services (999 or 112 in the UK and Europe, 911 in North America) or a crisis line (Samaritans on 116 123 in the UK and Ireland, 988 in the United States), and tell someone you trust. And if what you are facing is abuse, go back to the chapter Love with Limits: safety comes first.

An example

A man helps to lead a church youth group with another volunteer who criticises his talks sharply, often in front of the young people. He used to argue back, and lie awake afterwards. Now, when it happens, he breathes, prays one line, and says quietly, “Let us talk about that after the session.” Afterwards he asks what the concern was, and finds that one point is fair. He also asks that criticism be given in private in future. The next week he brings him a coffee. The friendship is not easy, but the group is no longer watching two leaders fight.

Hope: grace changed us

Paul tells Titus to teach Christians “to be gentle, and to show perfect courtesy toward all people” (Titus 3:2). The reason he gives is striking. “For we ourselves were once foolish, disobedient, led astray … passing our days in malice and envy, hated by others and hating one another. But when the goodness and loving kindness of God our Savior appeared, he saved us” (Titus 3:3–5). We were the difficult people. Kindness appeared, and it changed us.

The same grace can change the person you find hard. The churches once heard of Saul of Tarsus with astonishment: “He who used to persecute us is now preaching the faith he once tried to destroy” (Galatians 1:23). So we go on gently, for “God may perhaps grant them repentance” (2 Timothy 2:25). We are not promised that they will change. We are promised that God will finish what he has begun in us (Philippians 1:6), and that a day is coming when there will be no difficult people left, ourselves included. “When he appears we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3:2).

For reflection

Which of these tools do you most need in the moment? Who is the wise friend you can talk to, and are you seeking help or allies? Do you see any signs of bitterness taking root? What would you do tomorrow for your difficult person if you truly believed that grace could change them?
